newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy Dec PPI/WPI both seen up 0.2 PCT M/.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy Dec PPI/WPI both seen up 0.2 PCT M/.

text.p: Italy's December producer and wholesale prices are seen rising slightly on a monthly basis, reflecting an increase in energy and other raw material prices, a Reuter poll of analysts showed on Friday.
Average forecasts see December's Producer Price Index (PPI) up 0.2 percent month on month and 0.8 percent year on year from a 0.2 percent monthly rise and an 0.6 percent annual increase in November.

December's Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is seen on average rising 0.2 percent month on month and 1.6 percent year on year compared to a 0.2 percent month-on-month drop and a 1.7 percent yearly increase in November.
National statistics body ISTAT will publish the data on Tuesday February 18.
"The (PPI) data will reflect a significant increase in raw materials, especially petrol prices and other energy sources," said Paolo Casadio, analyst at Credito Italiano.

Martino Dolfini, analyst at Chase Manhattan Bank in Milan, said, "The increase in December is only caused by energy prices. In fact, core PPI, ex-food and energy, should come out unchanged monthly and down 0.5 percent yearly."
Bruno Rovelli, analyst at Bank of America in Milan, said that what weighs on the annual PPI data is a unfavourable comparison with December 1995.
In December 1995, producer prices were flat month-on-month and rose 6.5 percent yearly. Wholesale prices were up 0.3 percent monthly and 10.1 percent yearly.

"The latest Isco study showed that the disinflationary trend in Italy may be over," said Gianluca Sanna, analyst at Banco di Sardegna. "But this does not necessarily mean that we ought to expect price increases at any cost, because stagnating demand prevents producers from passing on price increases to consumers," Sanna added.
Analysts noted that since October state economic research body Isco's surveys on price trends have showed an expectation of an upward trend.

They attribute the increase in the WPI to higher raw materials prices. "In November, the month-on-month WPI drop was attributable to a fall in energy prices, but in December these prices started to rise again," said Alfredo Granata, analyst at Banca di Roma.
